choices.explanation: UDP does not itself provide reliable, ordered delivery.

questions.prompt: A site receives 2001:db8:7a00:a3f0::/60 and assigns one /64 to each VLAN. How many /64 subnets fit, and what is the last /64 prefix in this allocation?

choices.explanation: Four additional prefix bits create 16 combinations, not four.
The low hexadecimal digit of the fourth hextet varies from 0 through f.
a400 lies outside the /60 whose fourth hextet begins a3f.
A /60-to-/64 split adds four bits, not eight.

questions.explanation: The subnet count is 2^(64 − 60) = 16. The first three digits of the fourth hextet remain a3f; its last digit yields prefixes a3f0 through a3ff.

questions.prompt: An Ethernet interface explicitly uses modified EUI-64 to form its IPv6 interface identifier from MAC address 3C-52-82-AB-10-FE. What 64-bit interface identifier results?

choices.text: 3c52:82ff:feab:10fe
choices.explanation: This inserts ff:fe but leaves the U/L bit unchanged.

choices.text: 3d52:82ff:feab:10fe
choices.explanation: This changes the low-order bit instead of the U/L bit.

choices.text: 3e52:82ff:feab:10fe
choices.explanation: Insert ff:fe in the middle and XOR the first byte 3c with 02 to obtain 3e.

choices.text: 3e52:82ff:ffab:10fe
choices.explanation: The inserted bytes must be ff:fe, not ff:ff.

questions.explanation: Insert FF-FE between the third and fourth MAC octets, then invert the U/L bit in the first octet. The bytes become 3E-52-82-FF-FE-AB-10-FE. This question specifies EUI-64; IPv6 interfaces can use other identifier-generation methods.

questions.prompt: Which THREE IPv6 address classifications are correct? Select three.

choices.text: 2001:4860:1234::8 is link-local unicast
choices.explanation: This is global unicast space; link-local unicast begins with fe80::/10.

choices.text: fd12:3456:789a:1::8 is unique local unicast
choices.explanation: The fd prefix identifies the locally assigned part of fc00::/7.

choices.text: fe80::8 is link-local unicast
choices.explanation: It is in the link-local unicast prefix and is confined to its link.

choices.text: ff02::1 is global unicast
choices.explanation: An address beginning ff is multicast; the scope here is link-local.

choices.text: ff02::2 is multicast
choices.explanation: The ff prefix identifies multicast, and ff02::2 is the link-local all-routers group.

questions.explanation: The prefixes distinguish unique local, link-local, and multicast addresses. Unique local addresses can be routed within an organization, whereas link-local unicast addresses remain on their local link.

questions.prompt: Two service nodes at different sites advertise reachability to the same IPv6 anycast service address. Routing has converged, and a client sends one packet to that address. What does anycast provide?

choices.text: Delivery toward one service node according to the routing system’s selected path
choices.explanation: Routing selects a path to one instance of the shared service address.

choices.text: A copy of the packet delivered to both service nodes
choices.explanation: That describes group delivery, not anycast.

choices.text: Delivery to the physically closest service node regardless of routing policy
choices.explanation: Routing preference does not necessarily correspond to geographic distance.

choices.text: Delivery to the node with the lowest application response time, measured by anycast itself
choices.explanation: Anycast does not inherently measure application response time.

questions.explanation: Anycast presents the same service address from multiple locations. The network routes a packet toward one instance; its choice follows routing information and policy rather than an inherent geographic or application-latency measurement.

questions.prompt: A Windows client has the displayed configuration. Its VLAN uses 10.44.8.64/26, and the router interface serving that VLAN is 10.44.8.65. The client has no other adapter or manually added route. Which single client setting should be corrected to use that router for remote networks?

exhibit.content:
C:\> ipconfig /all

Ethernet adapter Ethernet:
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.44.8.70
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.192
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 10.44.8.1
   DNS Servers . . . . . . . . . . . : 10.44.8.90

choices.text: Change the IPv4 address to 10.44.8.64
choices.explanation: That is the VLAN subnet address, not a usable host address.

choices.text: Change the default gateway to 10.44.8.65
choices.explanation: It is the stated router interface and lies in the client’s .64–.127 subnet.

choices.text: Change the subnet mask to 255.255.255.0
choices.explanation: The configured /26 matches the VLAN design; widening it would misidentify remote addresses as local.

choices.text: Change the DNS server to 10.44.8.65
choices.explanation: Changing name resolution does not correct the default gateway.

questions.explanation: The address and mask match the VLAN, but the configured gateway .1 does not. Set the default gateway to the stated router interface .65.

questions.prompt: An administrator proposes hiding an SSID as a substitute for WPA2-Personal with AES-CCMP. Which TWO statements correctly distinguish these measures? Select two.

choices.text: Hiding the SSID does not provide encryption for user data
choices.explanation: SSID visibility is distinct from encrypting the wireless link.

choices.text: A hidden SSID guarantees that radio observers cannot discover the network name
choices.explanation: The name can still be discovered through wireless traffic.

choices.text: WPA2-Personal with AES-CCMP provides protection for wireless user-data confidentiality
choices.explanation: AES-CCMP protects transmitted data after the security association is established.

choices.text: Selecting a different RF channel performs the same cryptographic function as AES-CCMP
choices.explanation: Channel selection determines frequency use, not encryption.

choices.text: Once an SSID is hidden, compatible clients need no authentication configuration
choices.explanation: Hiding a name does not replace the configured authentication requirements.

questions.prompt: A design uses conventional virtual machines, Linux process containers inside one VM, and separate VRFs on a router for two tenants. The tenants use overlapping IPv4 prefixes; there is no route leaking or external interconnection. Which THREE statements correctly describe these technologies? Select three.

choices.text: Each conventional VM has its own guest operating-system kernel
choices.explanation: VMs provide separate guest OS instances, even when sharing physical hardware.

choices.text: The Linux process containers inside one VM share that VM’s kernel
choices.explanation: These containers isolate processes within their host guest OS.

choices.text: The two VRFs maintain separate routing and forwarding tables for the overlapping prefixes
choices.explanation: The ingress interface’s VRF distinguishes the routing contexts.

choices.text: A VRF resolves address overlap by automatically performing NAT
choices.explanation: VRFs separate forwarding contexts; they do not inherently translate addresses.

choices.text: Each Linux process container must boot another complete guest kernel
choices.explanation: Ordinary process containers share their host kernel rather than booting independent kernels.

questions.explanation: VMs virtualize machines; process containers isolate applications using a shared kernel; VRFs isolate Layer 3 forwarding contexts. These mechanisms can coexist because they isolate different resources.

questions.prompt: A switch’s only MAC entry was learned dynamically for 0066.7788.9900 on Gi1/0/3. Its aging timer is explicitly 300 seconds. choices.explanation: Learning uses the source MAC, not the destination MAC.

choices.explanation: An access port with a voice VLAN supports this phone-and-PC arrangement.

questions.prompt: On a Catalyst switch, Gi1/0/8 is an access port explicitly assigned to VLAN 30. An administrator deletes VLAN 30 from the local VLAN database without changing the interface configuration. What happens to that port?

choices.text: It automatically returns to VLAN 1.
choices.explanation: Deletion does not reset an explicit access VLAN assignment.

choices.text: It becomes a trunk using native VLAN 1.
choices.explanation: Deleting a VLAN does not change the port mode.

choices.text: It continues forwarding in VLAN 30 until the switch restarts.
choices.explanation: A deleted VLAN is not available for normal forwarding.

choices.text: It remains assigned to VLAN 30 and becomes inactive.
choices.explanation: The assignment persists; restoring the VLAN or assigning another existing VLAN restores its VLAN membership.

questions.explanation: VLAN 1 is the default Ethernet VLAN, but it is not an automatic fallback when an explicitly assigned VLAN is deleted. The port keeps its VLAN 30 assignment and cannot forward normally in that absent VLAN.

questions.prompt: R1 routes between VLANs 10 and 20 through an 802.1Q trunk. Both VLANs are active and permitted on the switch trunk; neither is native. Hosts use the shown subinterface addresses as their gateways. The physical link is up, and no ACLs apply. VLAN 10 hosts reach their gateway; VLAN 20 hosts cannot. Which change corrects the configuration?

exhibit.content:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 no ip address
 no shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.0.2.1 255.255.255.128
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 200
 ip address 192.0.2.129 255.255.255.128

choices.text: Change Gi0/0.20 to encapsulation dot1Q 20.
choices.explanation: The VLAN 20 gateway is currently bound to tag 200 instead of tag 20.

choices.text: Add a static route to 192.0.2.128/25 through Gi0/0.10.
choices.explanation: Routing cannot repair the wrong incoming VLAN classification; this subnet is already assigned locally.

choices.text: Change Gi0/0.10 to encapsulation dot1Q 20.
choices.explanation: That would misassign the working VLAN 10 gateway and leave Gi0/0.20 wrong.

choices.text: Configure the switch trunk with native VLAN 20.
choices.explanation: The design explicitly uses tagged VLAN 20; its router subinterface still expects VLAN 200.

questions.explanation: Subinterface numbers are labels; the encapsulation command selects the actual VLAN tag. Binding Gi0/0.20 to VLAN 20 makes its 192.0.2.129/25 gateway reachable from that VLAN.

questions.prompt: SW1 and SW2 have a working trunk. VLANs 10, 20, and 30 exist on both switches and are forwarding wherever permitted. SW1 allows all three; SW2 has the configuration shown. Which interface command on SW2 restores VLAN 30 connectivity while preserving the currently allowed VLANs?

interface GigabitEthernet1/0/48
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20

choices.text: switchport access vlan 30
choices.explanation: The access VLAN setting does not add traffic to an operational trunk.

choices.text: switchport trunk native vlan 30
choices.explanation: Changing the native VLAN does not add VLAN 30 to the allowed list.

choices.text: switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
choices.explanation: The add keyword extends the current list to 10,20,30.

choices.text: switchport trunk allowed vlan 30
choices.explanation: Without add, this replaces the list and removes VLANs 10 and 20.

questions.explanation: VLAN existence and trunk admission are separate requirements. The add form permits VLAN 30 without replacing the existing allowed list.
